solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Stress Musk's content to follow international court

indicators.note: to follow says the next piece comes after the court letters
content here means what is inside, so the outer letters of the name are dropped

parts.note: the surname of Elon Musk, the possessive ending set aside

explanation.surface: Elon Musk's posts are heading to an international court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'content' looks like satisfaction but means the inside of MUSK, which is US.
explanation.definitionFit: Ictus is the technical term in prosody for the rhythmic accent falling on a syllable.

clue.text: Causes of anxiety including money for everyone

parts.note: inc. is the abbreviation for including

explanation.surface: A worry that a universal cash handout will itself cause anxiety.
explanation.walkthrough: UBI, universal basic income, is a proposed payment to every citizen. Incubi are nightmare demons, so figuratively things that weigh on the mind.
explanation.definitionFit: An incubus is an oppressive burden or nightmare, so incubi are causes of anxiety.

clue.text: No longer going potty?

definitions.meaning: the surface hears 'no longer going mad'; the setter means a child who has stopped using something
not the slang for crazy but the child's pot, which a trained toddler has left behind for the lavatory

explanation.surface: Someone asking whether a person has regained their sanity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going potty' is British slang for going mad, which is the reading the surface pushes; the literal potty is the child's one.
explanation.definitionFit: Read literally, the clue describes a toddler who has graduated from a potty to the lavatory, which is exactly what training achieves.

clue.text: Obsessive admirer daughters tolerate

parts.note: a stan is an obsessive fan, from the Eminem song

explanation.surface: A parent wondering whether the daughters can put up with a superfan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Obsessive admirer' looks like the subject of the sentence, but it only supplies STAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, mostly heard in negatives: someone who can't bear a noise says they can't abide or put up with it.

clue.text: Back away from angry bluebottle, finally free after the setter's knocked over lab equipment

indicators.note: after says the rest of the pieces follow the setter's letters
knocked over means the two letters for the setter's are tipped round

parts.note: the setter is I, so the setter's is I'm

indicators.note: back away from means the back letter of the word for angry is dropped

parts.note: bluebottle is old slang for a policeman, a cop

indicators.note: finally picks the last letter of the word free

explanation.surface: Someone retreats from an angry fly after the setter has knocked over the lab kit.
explanation.walkthrough: A bluebottle is a fly in the surface but a police officer in the wordplay; CROSS loses its back letter to give CROS.
explanation.definitionFit: A microscope is the magnifying instrument found on every laboratory bench.

clue.text: Male dog, having lost lead, regularly peed and wandered aimlessly

indicators.note: having lost lead means the leading letter of the dog word is gone
regularly takes every other letter of the word peed

explanation.surface: A male dog slipped its lead, stopped to pee and wandered about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lead' looks like a dog lead, but it is the first letter of POOCH, leaving OOCH.
explanation.definitionFit: To mooch is to loiter or drift about with no clear purpose, an informal synonym.

clue.text: Established place for nuns on island on lake

parts.note: Iona, the Hebridean island off Mull

explanation.surface: A convent founded on an island in a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'Established' as 'founded', a verb about the convent, but it is the adjective: established ways are conventional ones. IONA is a Scottish island famous for its abbey.
explanation.definitionFit: Conventional practice is the established, accepted way of doing things.

clue.text: Defeat that hurts touring team, albeit depleted

indicators.note: touring means going round, so the cry goes around the other letters

parts.note: ouch is the cry for something that hurts

indicators.note: depleted empties both team and albeit, removing their insides and keeping only each word's outside letters

parts.note: taken as written; emptying each word leaves its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Losing to a touring side hurts, even though that side was below strength.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma is a red herring: depleted applies to both team and albeit, and the touring cry wraps what is left of them.
explanation.definitionFit: To outmatch an opponent is to prove superior and so beat them.

clue.text: Fiscal watchdog started by Conservative, a cold-blooded creature

parts.note: the UK's Office for Budget Responsibility

explanation.surface: A political jibe: the budget watchdog, set up by the Tories, is a cold-blooded snake.
explanation.walkthrough: The OBR is Britain's independent fiscal watchdog, created by a Conservative chancellor in 2010, so the surface is a fair political jab. 'A cold-blooded creature' works both as the snake and as the insult.
explanation.definitionFit: A cobra is a snake, and snakes are cold-blooded reptiles.

clue.text: Append electronic reference work about collection of Old Norse verse

indicators.note: turn the whole assembly about

parts.note: to cite is to refer to

explanation.surface: An instruction to add an online reference book about Norse poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reference work' pretends to be one thing, an encyclopaedia, but splits in two. Op. is the abbreviation for opus, used in numbering composers' works.
explanation.definitionFit: A factual description: the anthology preserved in the thirteenth-century Icelandic Codex Regius gathers mythological and heroic poems about Odin, Thor and Sigurd.

clue.text: Was theatrical dame disheartened, as I see it on reflection?

indicators.note: on reflection means the whole string is mirrored, read from the end
disheartened removes the heart of the word dame, keeping its outside letters

parts.note: as I see it is to me, run together

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a grand old actress was overdoing it on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: DE plus TOME gives DETOME, which read backwards is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To emote is to act out emotion in an exaggerated, stagey way.

clue.text: Aged parent went off, forgetting name

parts.note: TURNED (went off, like milk) without N for name

explanation.surface: An elderly parent who left, forgetting a name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aged parent' looks like one phrase for an old mum or dad; 'Aged' is the definition alone. 'Went off' means turned sour, as milk does.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as verbs in the past tense: cheese or whisky left for years grows older and ripens.

clue.text: Newspaper editor, one opening function for actor

parts.note: a rag is a disparaging word for a newspaper

explanation.surface: A newspaper editor opening a charity event for an actor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening function' reads as a gala launch; 'function' is the maths sense, TAN, which RAG, ED and I break open.
explanation.definitionFit: A tragedian is an actor who plays tragic roles.

clue.text: Nobel laureate and woman cycling north

indicators.note: cycling means letters go round from the front of the word to the back

parts.note: N is the compass abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: A Nobel winner and a woman are out cycling northwards.
explanation.walkthrough: Moving LA from the front of LADY to the back gives DYLA.
explanation.definitionFit: Bob Dylan won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2016 for his songwriting.

clue.text: Current sweetheart removing old underwear introduces villainous character

indicators.note: the underwear comes first and introduces the rest

parts.note: I is the symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: A current partner who is throwing out the old thermal underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current sweetheart' reads as someone's present partner; 'Current' gives I on its own. Long John Silver is the one-legged pirate of Treasure Island.
explanation.definitionFit: Long John Silver is the villain of Stevenson's Treasure Island.

clue.text: Security organisation with cracking feature film

explanation.surface: A security body with a hit feature film on its hands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cracking feature film' sounds like a rave review, with 'cracking' as British praise; here it means breaking open, and 'feature' is part of a face.
explanation.definitionFit: Chinatown is the 1974 film noir starring Jack Nicholson.

clue.text: Board pay for party game

parts.note: a board is a table, as in board and lodging
to foot the bill is to pay it
a ball is a dance party

explanation.surface: A company board agreeing to pay for a party game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party game' looks like a single phrase; 'party' gives BALL and 'game' is the definition. Table football is foosball.
explanation.definitionFit: Table football is a game played with rods of little footballers.

clue.text: Extent of study most of the book initiates

parts.note: to read a subject at university is to study it

explanation.surface: How widely a student must read: most of the set text before starting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extent of study' reads as a single phrase about a syllabus; only 'Extent' defines. To read a subject is the British university sense of study it.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the width or range of something, as when a critic praises how widely a scholar's knowledge reaches.

clue.text: Sending forth European delegating authority to missing Democrat

explanation.surface: A European handing power to a Democrat who has gone missing.
explanation.walkthrough: To mandate is to give authority to someone; the D then drops out.
explanation.definitionFit: Emanating means issuing or sending forth, as light emanates from a lamp.

clue.text: Using the local tongue, river guide enthrals husband

indicators.note: to enthral once meant to hold in thrall, captive

explanation.surface: A river guide who charms a husband by speaking the local language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'River guide' sounds like a boatman; 'river' belongs to the definition and 'guide' is REIN. The Rhein is the Rhine in German, the local tongue.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhein is the German name of the Rhine, the river as locals say it.

clue.text: Son ran this person's drinking spot — he'll try to stop thieves

parts.note: to spot something is to detect it
I'VE: this person, the setter, has

explanation.surface: A son running the setter's local bar, and a note that he will try to stop thieves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drinking spot' reads as a bar, but 'spot' is a verb here, meaning notice, and 'drinking' only dresses the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: a plain-clothes guard employed by a shop, whose job is catching shoplifters before they leave.

clue.text: White wine imbibed by glamorous setter

indicators.note: the answer has been swallowed by the words that follow

explanation.surface: A glamorous crossword setter sipping white wine.
explanation.walkthrough: Roussette is a white grape and wine of Savoie; it straddles the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: an Alpine appellation from Savoie in eastern France, made from the Altesse grape.

clue.text: Did meditation, free of concerning wobbles

indicators.note: to be free of something is to be rid of it, so ON leaves MEDITATION
the remaining letters shake into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone who meditated but was still anxious and shaky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Did meditation' reads as a verb and its object; 'Did' alone is the definition, as in 'she did the Queen', meaning impersonated.
explanation.definitionFit: To do someone, as an impressionist does, is to imitate them.

clue.text: Consecrates roads in Barking

indicators.note: barking means mad, so the letters go wild

explanation.surface: A bishop blessing new roads in Barking, a town in east London.
explanation.walkthrough: Barking is a district of east London, and the capital letter makes it a place; in the wordplay it is the slang for mad.
explanation.definitionFit: To ordain is to consecrate someone as a priest.

clue.text: Briefly look over painter's note in shock

parts.note: to scan is to look over quickly

explanation.surface: Glancing at a painter's note and being shocked by it.
explanation.walkthrough: Dalí is the usual crossword painter; his note leaves one scandalised.
explanation.definitionFit: To scandalise is to shock people by offending their sense of propriety.

clue.text: Something divisive that may put you off your stroke?

definitions.meaning: the political sense: a topic chosen to split the other side

definitions.text: may put you off your stroke?
definitions.meaning: the golf sense: a problem with your wedge, a lofted club

explanation.surface: A golfer blaming a fault in the wedge for a bad shot.
explanation.walkthrough: A wedge issue is a political topic used to split an opponent's supporters. The question mark flags the golf reading: a wedge is a club, and an issue with it would spoil your stroke.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: American political slang for a topic that splits a coalition, and literally trouble with a golfer's lofted club.

clue.text: Appraisal of mixture of olive and tuna pasta, ultimately

indicators.note: a mixture blends ingredients together, so the fodder's letters are stirred into a new order
ultimately means in the end, so only the end letter of pasta counts

explanation.surface: A food critic's verdict on an olive and tuna pasta dish.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a restaurant review, and an appraisal is exactly what a review is.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both nouns name a judgement of worth, such as a manager's yearly review of staff performance.

clue.text: Laid into women's novel lacking in depth

indicators.note: the letters take a new form

explanation.surface: A critic savaging a women's novel for having shallow characters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' is set up as a book, and it is the anagram instruction. A two-dimensional character is exactly the complaint the surface's critic makes.
explanation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: flat shapes have width and height but no third axis, so shallow fictional characters get called this.

clue.text: Ulterior motive that's characteristic of Häagen-Dazs?

definitions.meaning: the brand name hides AGENDA: HäAGEN-DAzs

explanation.surface: A suspicion that an ice-cream brand has a secret motive.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half is a crossword joke: the letters AGENDA are literally hidden inside Häagen-Dazs.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for a concealed purpose, and literally true of the ice-cream brand, whose spelling conceals those six letters.

clue.text: Declined to leave excellent books about New England

indicators.note: 'about' in its sense of around

parts.note: OT = Old Testament, a set of books

explanation.surface: Someone who refused to part with first-rate books on New England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Declined' looks like 'refused'; it means deteriorated. OT is the Old Testament.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom meaning deteriorated badly, as a neglected garden or a failing business does.

clue.text: Shape of old Indian city outlined by His Majesty

indicators.note: 'outlined by' means the pieces sit inside the royal abbreviation

parts.note: Agra is the Indian city of the Taj Mahal

explanation.surface: An old Indian city's map is traced by the King.
explanation.definitionFit: A hexagram is a six-pointed star figure, a geometric shape.

clue.text: Brilliant to get shot of island group

indicators.note: to get shot of something is to be rid of it

parts.note: 'that's genius' is informal British praise for something brilliant
I = island; this is the letter removed

explanation.surface: A cheer at finally being rid of a group of islands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Island group' looks like one phrase, an archipelago; 'group' is the definition. 'Genius' as an adjective (that's genius!) is British slang for brilliant.
explanation.definitionFit: A technical sense from biology: the rank above species, grouping closely related organisms such as lions and tigers.

clue.text: Test digital assistant installed by groups of schoolchildren lacking boundaries

indicators.note: something installed is fitted inside a place

parts.note: FORMS (school classes) without the F and S at its edges

explanation.surface: Schools installing a digital assistant in classrooms to test pupils.
explanation.walkthrough: A form is a school class in Britain. ALEXA sits inside what is left of FORMS.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by type: an examination answered out loud to an examiner rather than written down, as viva candidates face.

clue.text: Longed to grab bite for walrus?

parts.note: a nip is a small bite

explanation.surface: A walrus longing to take a bite.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark says the walrus is only one example: pinnipeds are the seals, sea lions and walruses.
explanation.definitionFit: A walrus is a pinniped, a fin-footed marine mammal.

clue.text: Can worker rebuild ropier coffins?

indicators.note: the letters are rebuilt in another order

explanation.surface: Asking whether an undertaker's worker can remake some shoddy coffins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' reads as the verb 'is able to'; it is slang for prison. Ropey is British slang for poor quality.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang: American usage calls a jail 'the can', so a warder employed there is someone working in it.

clue.text: Initially, this grift sat awkwardly

indicators.note: the letters sit awkwardly, out of order

explanation.surface: Someone uneasy about a con from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: A grift is a swindle; the surface says the scam felt wrong from the beginning.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for the opening impression, before closer inspection changes one's view, as in love on a first meeting.

clue.text: Thoroughly popular Irish parliament hosting drug summit at last

indicators.note: 'at last' means at the very end, so only the final letter of summit is used

explanation.surface: The Irish parliament hosting a summit on drugs to popular acclaim.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dáil is the lower house of the Irish parliament; E and T go inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: An adverbial phrase: covering every particular, as a report examined point by point rather than skimmed.

clue.text: Congratulations puzzle lieutenant, more than half-cut

explanation.surface: Congratulating a lieutenant who is rather drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-cut' is British slang for drunk, and 'more than half-cut' reads as very drunk; it means half of OVER.
explanation.definitionFit: Mazel tov is a Hebrew and Yiddish expression of congratulations.

clue.text: Either four or six absent from unimportant court proceedings

indicators.note: someone absent from a place is missing from it, so the numeral goes missing from the word

parts.note: Roman IV (four), or VI (six) — the letters removed

explanation.surface: A trivial court case where four or six people failed to turn up.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is candid that it does not matter which: the IV and VI in TRIVIAL are the same letters, so dropping either leaves TRIAL.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the hearing where a judge or jury examines evidence and decides guilt.

clue.text: Company called the French heads of inventory and sales for instrument

indicators.note: 'heads of' takes the first letter of inventory and of sales, skipping the joining and

explanation.surface: A company rang the French office about stock and sales figures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heads of' covers both inventory and sales; the 'and' between them only joins them and gives no letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The cor anglais is a woodwind instrument, a larger relative of the oboe.

clue.text: Computer user misused legal authority

indicators.note: the letters are used wrongly, in the wrong order

explanation.surface: A computer user who has abused legal powers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Misused legal authority' reads as abuse of power, but 'misused' shuffles the first two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the highest tribunal in many countries, whose rulings bind every lower judge.

clue.text: Streamer perhaps posted car crashes

indicators.note: the letters crash and come out jumbled

explanation.surface: A streamer posting car-crash videos online.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' marks a podcaster as one kind of streamer, a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: A podcaster is one example of someone who streams content online.

clue.text: Innovative companies stir proud southern founders

indicators.note: to founder is to collapse or sink, so the words before it fall apart into a new order

explanation.surface: Pioneering start-ups whose founders are stirring up the proud South.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stir' and 'founders' both look like business talk; 'stir' is fodder and 'founders' is the verb, collapse, that scrambles it.
explanation.definitionFit: Business jargon: start-ups whose new technology upends an established market, as streaming did to video rental.

clue.text: Sort of backing singers Danny is periodically employing to begin with

indicators.note: backing means the selected letters are read in reverse order
periodically takes every other letter of the run singers Danny is

parts.note: every other letter of these three words, starting with the first

indicators.note: to begin with picks the first letter of the word employing

explanation.surface: Danny is hiring a sort of backing group to start off with.
explanation.walkthrough: The odd letters of singers Danny is give SNESANI; backwards that is INASENS, and E from employing finishes it.
explanation.definitionFit: In a sense is an idiom hedging a claim, meaning partly or to some extent.

clue.text: Continues to be close by university residence

indicators.note: the pieces sit next to each other

parts.note: a res is a student residence hall

explanation.surface: Staying on near the university halls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close by' reads as 'near'; 'close' is the noun, the END.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the third person: a tradition that survives for centuries persists and lasts.

clue.text: Artist's hit that felt endless

parts.note: to rap is to strike sharply

indicators.note: endless strips the end letters from each of that and felt, leaving their insides

parts.note: taken as written; each word loses both its end letters

explanation.surface: A painter's blow felt as if it would never stop.
explanation.walkthrough: THAT without its ends is HA and FELT without its ends is EL; the 's is a link meaning is.
explanation.definitionFit: Raphael was the High Renaissance Italian painter of the Sistine Madonna and the School of Athens.

clue.text: Notice car stop, probed by Republican government

indicators.note: a probe is pushed into something

parts.note: a station is a stop on a line

explanation.surface: A notice about a car stopped by the Republican government.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Car stop' reads as a traffic stop; it is MINI and STATION, with R pushed into STATION.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, especially in American usage: the Biden or Reagan years name the executive branch in power.

clue.text: Rodent, one biting hard shrub

indicators.note: teeth close round what they bite

explanation.surface: A rodent gnawing on a tough shrub.
explanation.walkthrough: Rhatany is an obscure South American shrub whose root was used in medicine; the wordplay is the way in.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhatany is a South American shrub of the genus Krameria.

clue.text: Drink mentioned down under rock band picked up

indicators.note: under in a down clue puts the following piece below the band's letters
picked up in a down clue means the band's name is read from bottom to top

parts.note: R.E.M. is the American rock band

indicators.note: mentioned means the word for down is spoken rather than spelt

parts.note: low means down, and said aloud it matches the end of the wine's name

explanation.surface: A drink is mentioned in Australia while a rock band picks up a request.
explanation.walkthrough: 'down under' looks like Australia, but down is the word said aloud and under places it beneath MER; the final T is silent in the French name.
explanation.definitionFit: Merlot is a red wine grape variety and the wine made from it.

clue.text: Small instrument out of tune

explanation.surface: A little instrument that won't stay in tune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small instrument' reads as a single thing, a piccolo perhaps; it is S plus HARP.
explanation.definitionFit: A note that is sharp is pitched too high, out of tune.

clue.text: Second corporation acquiring large shaft

parts.note: corporation is jocular British slang for a pot belly, a tum

explanation.surface: A second company buying a large shaft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corporation' looks like a company; in old slang it means a big belly, TUM. A stulm is a horizontal mine passage.
explanation.definitionFit: A stulm is an adit or level shaft driven into a mine.

clue.text: Manages courses in agronomy, partly retired

indicators.note: the answer lies in the words
retired means withdrawn, going backwards
only part of the words is used

explanation.surface: A retired farmer who now runs courses in agronomy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Partly retired' reads as semi-retired; it says the letters are a part and run backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To organise something is to manage it.

clue.text: Some bemoan a horrible biblical character

indicators.note: some of the letters give the answer

explanation.surface: Complaining about a dreadful figure from the Bible.
explanation.walkthrough: Nahor is Abraham's brother (and grandfather) in Genesis, obscure enough that the hidden word is the way in.
explanation.definitionFit: Nahor is a figure in Genesis, brother of Abraham.

clue.text: Somewhat advanced temperature gun

explanation.surface: A gun that is running rather hot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Somewhat advanced' reads as a single phrase; 'Somewhat' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A trifle means slightly, somewhat: a trifle tired.

clue.text: Man in pub recalled treatment for addiction

indicators.note: called back, so read backwards

explanation.surface: A man in a pub remembering his time in treatment.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a drinker remembering rehab; 'recalled' is really a reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: Short for rehabilitation, the clinic programme that helps people recover from dependence on drink or drugs.

clue.text: Running event in rural Oman that collapsed

indicators.note: the letters collapse into a new order

explanation.surface: A desert race in rural Oman that ended with runners collapsing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Collapsed' fits the surface, a runner collapsing in desert heat, and is also the anagram instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: An ultramarathon is a running race longer than a marathon.

clue.text: Introduction to guerrilla soldiers with big guns, reportedly capricious with figures

indicators.note: an introduction comes at the start, so only the opening letter of guerrilla is used
what follows is heard, not spelt

explanation.surface: Guerrilla fighters with heavy guns who behave unpredictably.
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Artillery are the British Army's gunners. 'With figures' means illustrated with diagrams.
explanation.definitionFit: Graphical means using graphs or figures.

clue.text: Just married on visiting cathedral city

explanation.surface: Newlyweds visiting a cathedral city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just married' reads as newlyweds; 'Just' is the definition. ELY is a small English cathedral city, a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as adverbs: 'it was merely a scratch' and 'it was only a scratch' say the same.

clue.text: Earl bad-tempered, eating mixed nuts every so often in a greedy manner

indicators.note: 'eating' means the bad-tempered word takes the other letters inside it
'every so often' takes alternate letters of the words mixed nuts

explanation.surface: An irritable earl eats a bowl of mixed nuts, gobbling them down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mixed' looks like the anagram signal, but it is fodder: the even letters of MIXED NUTS give IENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Esurient means hungry or greedy, so the adverb describes eating voraciously.

clue.text: Bordering on raucous, entering bar for pop

indicators.note: 'entering' means the edge letters go into the bar word

parts.note: but means except, as does bar

indicators.note: 'Bordering on' takes the outer letters of raucous

explanation.surface: A noisy crowd almost bursts into a bar to buy fizzy drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bar' and 'pop' suggest a pub and a soft drink; bar is BUT, as in 'all bar one'.
explanation.definitionFit: To burst is to pop, as a balloon does.
